children: To the Editor: Congress has ultimate authority over tariffs, not the president, per Article I of the Constitution ("What a Democratic Congress Would Mean for Wall Street," Cover Story, Oct. 22). Any tariff authority the president has can be rescinded. Whether Congress will do that depends on a lot, but technically it can have the final say over tariffs if it wants to. And I'm sure the Democrats will consider this if a blue wave materializes.

To the Editor: Raising the capital-gains exclusion from $500,000 to $1 million is long overdue. I don't know what percentage of those who want to sell their homes are holding back because they have gains in excess of $500,000. Regardless, which of our politicians will have the courage to vote in favor of such legislation, knowing that they will be attacked for selling out to the wealthy?

To the Editor: "Mixed" results is a very generous characterization ("The Trump Economy in 7 Charts," Oct. 22). The main positive here is stock market performance, but that's an expected result of the massive deficit spending engendered by tax cuts. GDP growth is below the trend of the past 45 years, and hardly "robust." Job creation has been quite weak, per the chart.
It's OK to Be a Renter

To the Editor: Homeownership isn't necessarily slipping away. Americans may simply be unwilling to move, compromise, or consider renting ("Homeownership Helped Make America. It's Slipping Away for Millions," Oct. 18.) Restrictive zoning and glacial permitting processes deserve much of the blame, but so does our collective fixation on living in America's most expensive markets. Nebraska may not offer New York's amenities, and Kansas may lack California's climate, but both provide affordable housing. Government should remove barriers to building, and families should look beyond a handful of high-cost metro areas. Most important, renting is often the financially rational choice, even if decades of real estate industry marketing have convinced Americans otherwise.
Jonathan I. Shenkman West Hempstead, N.Y.

To the Editor: As a 73-year-old retiree, options ETFs give me exposure to growth plus meaningful income with better returns than traditional fixed income ("Options ETFs Are Booming. Beware the Trade-Offs," Oct. 22). Some use Section 1256 contracts, tax-loss harvesting, and constructive return of capital as a tax classification, and some sell put options, so the upside isn't capped.
